{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

The main practice for Chapter 18 is Elaf's complete project, which you can download at the bottom of this page and run on your own computer: from the raw survey export to a results chapter. The exercises below practise the small pieces that make a results chapter: helper functions for reporting, a sample table, and sentences with numbers taken from models. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
students      <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters     <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    stress_4 = 6 - stress_4,
    stress   = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    support  = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(student_id, stress, support)
study <- students |>
  left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1), join_by(student_id))
```

## Helper functions for reporting

### Exercise 1: Mean and SD in one string

Theses report "mean (SD)" with one decimal place. Complete the function, and use it on the students' ages.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
mean_sd <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), ______(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}
mean_sd(study$age)
mean_sd(study$wellbeing)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean_sd <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

"29.7 (4.8)" and "60.5 (12.0)". Written once, the function formats every mean in the thesis the same way.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Formatting p-values

APA style writes p-values without a leading zero, with three decimals, and "p < .001" for very small values. Complete the function and test it.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
format_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < ______) "p < .001" else paste("p =", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
}
format_p(0.0004)
format_p(0.0321)
format_p(0.5)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
format_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) "p < .001" else paste("p =", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
}
```

"p < .001", "p = .032", and "p = .500". `sub("^0", "", ...)` removes the zero at the start of the text.
:::
:::

## The sample table

### Exercise 3: One column of Table 1

`describe()` builds one column of a sample table for any group of students. Use it for the PhD students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
mean_sd <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
describe <- function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Characteristic = c("Students", "Age, mean (SD)", "Women", "Part-time"),
    Value = c(nrow(d), mean_sd(d$age), percent(d$gender == "Female"),
              percent(d$study_mode == "Part-time"))
  )
}
describe(filter(study, programme == "______"))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
describe(filter(study, programme == "PhD"))
```

174 PhD students, with an average age of 34.2 (SD 5.1). Running `describe(study)` gives the column for all students, with no copied code.
:::
:::

## Sentences from models

### Exercise 4: The effect of sleep on GPA

Fit the chapter's regression, then report the sleep coefficient and its 95% confidence interval in a sentence.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
gpa_model <- lm(gpa ~ sleep_hours + study_hours + stress + support, data = study)
b  <- coef(gpa_model)["sleep_hours"]
ci <- confint(gpa_model)["______", ]
sprintf("Each extra hour of sleep was associated with a GPA %.2f points higher (95%% CI %.2f to %.2f).",
        b, ci[1], ci[2])
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ci <- confint(gpa_model)["sleep_hours", ]
```

"Each extra hour of sleep was associated with a GPA 0.11 points higher (95% CI 0.08 to 0.13)." In `sprintf()`, `%%` writes a single percent sign.
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: An odds ratio in a sentence

Fit the logistic regression for considering dropout and report the odds ratio for stress.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
dropout_model <- glm(I(considering_dropout == "Yes") ~ stress + support + financial_worry,
                     data = study, family = binomial)
odds_ratio <- exp(coef(dropout_model)["______"])
sprintf("Each one-point increase in stress multiplied the odds of considering dropout by %.1f.",
        odds_ratio)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
odds_ratio <- exp(coef(dropout_model)["stress"])
```

About 3.8 with this simpler model (the chapter's model, which also includes employment and study mode, gives 3.6). Always say which variables the model adjusted for.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Check before you report

Before reporting a model, check how many students it used. `nobs()` gives the number of observations; compare it with the number of students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
gpa_model <- lm(gpa ~ sleep_hours + study_hours + stress + support, data = study)
nobs(gpa_model)
nrow(study) - ______
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
nrow(study) - nobs(gpa_model)
```

13 students were left out because at least one of the model's variables was missing. A thesis reports the number of students each model used (*n* = 587 here), and Chapter 5 discusses whether leaving them out could bias the results.
:::
:::

## Download the Chapter 18 project

Elaf's complete project: the raw export in `data-raw/`, the numbered scripts in `R/` (cleaning, then analysis), and `results.qmd`, which renders the results chapter with every number taken from the code. `exercises.txt` suggests changes to make, and the last exercise starts your own project with the same structure.

- Or type this one line in RStudio's Console:

```r
usethis::use_course("https://polla-fattah.github.io/R4NTR/playground/chapter18.zip")
```
:::
